title: Muscles
description: Conditions affecting the masticatory and orofacial muscles — pain, restricted opening, and muscle-driven deformity.

problems.description: Dull aching pain around the jaw and temple, worse on waking or by end of day, with limited or painful opening and no obvious dental cause.
problems.etiology:
The joint itself is anatomically normal — this is an extra-articular problem driven by muscle tension and spasm [1]. The leading theory is that stress-induced parafunctional habits (bruxism, clenching) generate sustained masticatory muscle contraction, which lowers the pain threshold and produces the characteristic dull, heavy, diffuse ache [2]. This is compatible with the condition's frequent association with depression, tension headache, irritable bowel syndrome, and fibromyalgia [3].

The reason it's so hard to pin down: causes are multifactorial and poorly understood. Muscle tension, local and central pain processing, and psychological response to stress all play a part [1]. It doesn't explain every case — some patients identify no particular stress, and the aetiology in that group remains unclear [3].

Parafunction (bruxism, clenching) is the mechanism that bridges stress and muscle symptoms. It should be noted as a contributing factor here, but bruxism as a standalone condition is classified under the psychological origin.
problems.presentation:
What the patient typically says:

- Dull, heavy, diffuse ache over the side of the face [1].
- Pain varies in severity — either worst in the morning and slowly easing, or worsening progressively through the day [1].
- Limited or painful opening.

What you'll find on examination:

- Pain on palpation over the muscles of mastication and/or the preauricular region [4].
- The masticatory muscles are often tense and tender to palpation; joint movements are often painful [1].
- Clicking may be present if there is a component of internal derangement — clicking commonly occurs at 2–3 mm of tooth separation on opening and sometimes closing [4].
- Look for signs of parafunction: masseteric hypertrophy on clenching, attrition on occlusal surfaces [5].
problems.results:
- **Mouth opening**: restricted opening is common, but the joint movements possible differ from intra-articular disease. In extra-articular causes, translation is intact and lateral and protrusive movements are usually unaffected [6].
- **Palpation**: generalized bilateral tenderness of the muscles of mastication — masseter, lateral pterygoid, temporalis [7].
- **Radiograph/imaging**: joint structure is normal. Plain radiography, DPT, and MRI show no articular abnormality [8]. This is a diagnostic point: the imaging being clear in the context of significant muscle tenderness supports a myofascial rather than intra-articular aetiology.
- **No inflammatory markers**: blood tests (CRP, ESR, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP) would be within normal limits, helping to rule out inflammatory arthritis [8].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The thing that separates myofascial TMD from its close neighbours:

- **Normal joint architecture**: unlike internal derangement (anteriorly displaced disc causing mechanical obstruction) or TMJ osteoarthrosis (condylar erosion, crepitus, X-ray changes), myofascial pain has a structurally intact joint on imaging [1, 8].
- **Lateral movement preserved**: in intra-articular trismus, translation is blocked in all directions; in extra-articular muscle-based restriction, lateral and protrusive movements are usually unaffected [6].
- **Prevalence and self-limiting nature**: affects approximately 50% of the population at some point in their lives [9]. Most cases are self-limiting — simple conservative measures succeed in up to 80% of patients [10].
- **Bruxism/parafunction link**: masseteric hypertrophy and attrition are peripheral clues that parafunction is loading the system [5].
problems.treatment:
Conservative measures first — they work in ~80% of cases [10].

**First-line (every dentist can provide):**

- **Reassurance and explanation**: advise on the benign, frequently self-limiting course. Identify stressed or depressed patients by gentle history-taking; an information leaflet helps [11].
- **Simple analgesia, rest, and gentle heat**: patient compliance at home is what drives recovery, more than who prescribes it [12].
- **Splint therapy**: upper or lower, hard or soft. The aims are to reduce bruxism and joint load, and increase the gap between condyle and fossa. Wear as often as possible (nights and evenings especially) and reassess after 4–6 weeks [13].
- **Remedial exercises**: physiotherapy with short-wave diathermy and ultrasound is an option, again dependent on patient compliance [12].

**Drug therapy (for refractory cases):**

- Tricyclics (nortriptyline, dosulepin) have analgesic and muscle-relaxant effects independent of their antidepressant action [14]. Dothiepin: initially 75 mg nocte, up to 150 mg daily; half-dose in the elderly [15].
- Benzodiazepines act as both a muscle relaxant and an anxiolytic. Diazepam: 2 mg tds, maximum 30 mg in divided daily doses [16].
- Chlorpromazine 10 mg tds is sometimes used instead of diazepam in TMD, with the same side effect profile [17].

**If no improvement within 3 months**: do not persist with ineffective treatment; refer to a specialist [10].
problems.prognosis: The condition is frequently self-limiting [11]. Simple conservative management succeeds in approximately 80% of patients [10]. If symptoms remain problematic after about 6 months, referral to a specialist is appropriate [18].

citations.quote: Temporomandibular joint disorder with myofascial pain is part of a group of TMJ disorders in which masticatory muscle pain predominates. The classification and nomenclature is contentious and complex, and the spectrum includes overlapping conditions from local to generalized myalgia. It is an extra-articular condition, and the joint is anatomically normal. This condition is often called temporomandibular joint pain–dysfunction syndrome, inappropriately suggesting that the condition is one of the joint. The patient reports a dull, heavy, diffuse ache over the side of the face, and the pain tends to vary in severity. Classically, one of two pain patterns is seen: pain being worst in the morning and slowly easing or pain that worsens progressively during the day. The masticatory muscles are often tense and tender to palpation, and joint movements are often painful. The causes are multifactorial and poorly understood. However, it seems that muscle tension/spasm, local and central pain processing and psychological response to stress all play a part.
To date, the concept of stress-induced parafunctional habits (bruxism, clenching) causing pain and spasm in the masticatory apparatus coupled with a ↓ pain threshold has seemed the most reasonable.

This is compatible with the observed high association with depression, back pain, tension headache, migraine, irritable bowel syndrome, and fibromyalgia. It does not, however, explain the cause in those patients who can identify no different levels of stress in their lives nor does it help explain the high incidence of internal derangement of the meniscus.

Pain, clicking, locking, crepitus, and trismus are the classical signs and symptoms. Some patients may be clinically depressed but most are not. Pain is elicited by palpation over the muscles of mastication &/or the preauricular region. Clicking commonly occurs at 2–3mm of tooth separation on opening and sometimes closing. This is due to the meniscus being displaced anteriorly on translation of the head of the condyle and then returning to its usual position (the click). A lock is when it does not return.

The pain is almost certainly caused by a cracked cusp or crown. The presence of masseteric hypertrophy and attrition on the occlusal surfaces of the teeth would suggest a parafunctional habit that could predispose to cracked tooth syndrome.
In extra-articular causes, the joint itself is normal, and thus, although opening can be restricted, translation occurs, and the lateral and protrusive movements are usually unaffected.
On palpation, there is tenderness over the right mandibular condyle and generalized bilateral tenderness of the muscles of mastication on the right – the masseter, lateral pterygoid and temporalis.

Laboratory tests: In this case, it would be expected that all laboratory test results would be within the normal range. Blood tests such as a complete blood count, Cross-reactive protein level, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, rheumatoid factor, anticyclical citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) and an autoantibody screen can help rule out other possible causes such as septic or rheumatoid arthritis.
Affects ~50% of the population at some time in their lives. F > M. Onset 20–30yrs of age.

These three simple measures should relieve symptoms in ~80% of patients and identify those needing referral to a specialist (Fig. 11.7). Do not persist with ineffective Rx if symptoms have not improved within 3 months.

Advice as to the nature of the problem and its benign and frequently self-limiting course is all that many patients require. Do not create a problem where there is none! This is also the time to take a gentle but thorough social and family history to identify clinically depressed patients or those with significant stress. An information leaflet is helpful.
Whether these are given by the dentist, physiotherapist (in the form of short-wave diathermy and US), or ancillary staff is unimportant, as the crucial part is the patient compliance at home.

Upper/lower, hard/soft have all been used with varying success. The initial aim of a splint is to (i) show something is being done (placebo); (ii) ↓ bruxism and joint load; and (iii) ↑ the gap between condyle and fossa, whereby the disc may be freed. A simple, full-coverage upper or lower splint should be worn as often as possible, nights and evenings especially, and reassessed after 4–6 weeks.
Nortriptyline, dosulepin, and related compounds have been demonstrated to have analgesic and muscle relaxant effects independent of their antidepressant effect.

It has, however, been demonstrated to be of value in the Rx of 'facial arthromyalgia' (a composite group of TMD and atypical facial-pain patients). Dose: initially 75mg nocte, ↑ to 150mg daily if needed. Half-dose in elderly.

A benzodiazepine may also be a valuable adjunct in the management of TMD, where it acts as both a muscle relaxant and an anxiolytic. Dose for anxiety/TMD: 2mg tds, maximum 30mg in divided daily doses.
Sometimes used instead of diazepam in TMD. It has the same side effect profile. Dose: 10mg tds, ↑ to maximum of 100mg daily, in divided doses.

In primary care, assessment and diagnosis should be undertaken, and appropriate habit modification, simple analgesic advice and bite splints can be appropriate treatments. If the symptoms remain problematic after approximately 6 months, then referral to a specialist should be considered.

problems.description: Progressive inability to open the mouth fully, developing gradually over months to years, with pale or mottled buccal mucosa in a patient of South Asian origin who chews betel quid.
problems.etiology:
Chronic and progressive scarring of oral connective tissue caused by betel quid (areca nut) chewing [1]. The mechanism: elevated copper from areca nut upregulates lysyl oxidase, which crosslinks collagen, increasing fibrosis [1]. The fibrosis involves the submucosa and eventually the deep muscle, making the lips, cheeks, and tongue progressively immobile [1, 2].

Adding tobacco to areca nut and slaked lime increases the risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma on top of the existing fibrosis [1]. The habit is addictive due to alkaloids in areca nut; it is embedded in the cultural and social customs of many South Asian communities [3].
problems.presentation:
Earliest features:

- Burning of the mucosa and roughness, sometimes described as 'tiny vesicles' [4]. These are non-specific but should raise suspicion in any betel quid user.

Established disease:

- Gradual, progressive limitation of mouth opening. The patient may report difficulty eating or toothbrushing [5].
- Restriction of tongue movement and reduced ability to protrude the tongue [6].
- Pale or mottled buccal and labial mucosa. Thin white hard fibrous bands run vertically below the mucosa, visible and palpable on examination [7].
- Some areas may appear red and atrophic [7].
problems.results:
- **Maximum voluntary mouth opening**: measure interincisal distance. Normal is approximately 35 mm; in established disease it may be 17 mm or less [8]. This is the baseline from which to judge progression.
- **Tenderness**: no tenderness of the TMJ or muscles of mastication — this distinguishes it from myofascial TMD and intra-articular disease [9].
- **Biopsy**: fibrosis of connective tissue with atrophic overlying epithelium. Deeper tissue shows fibrosis replacing tissue between epithelium and underlying muscle; superficial muscle fibres become atrophic and are replaced by fibrous tissue [10]. Dysplasia may be present.
- Approximately one-third of patients have concurrent oral white patches; dysplasia is found in up to 16% of the mucosa on biopsy [11].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
Oral submucous fibrosis produces trismus via a different mechanism from every other cause:

- **Mechanism**: fibrous bands in the submucosa — not muscle spasm, not intra-articular disease, not infection. The joint is normal; there are no articular clicks or crepitus [9].
- **Unlike myofascial TMD**: no muscle tenderness, no relationship to stress, no morning-vs-evening pain pattern.
- **Unlike radiotherapy-induced fibrosis**: absence of a history of head and neck irradiation [12].
- The combination of betel quid habit + pale fibrous bands + progressive restriction is virtually diagnostic [6]. Betel quid use should always be asked about in patients of South Asian origin presenting with trismus.
problems.treatment:
No treatment reverses established fibrosis, so the aims are prevention of complications and detection of malignancy [13].

**Habit cessation**: the single most important intervention. Address both areca nut and tobacco. The habit is addictive and culturally embedded — health education may need to extend to other family members [14].

**Mouth opening exercises**: if patients are committed, they may be spared the worst effects of extreme trismus. Best results are in those with relatively localised disease at diagnosis [13].

**Monitor for malignancy**: all abnormal mucosa requires biopsy. Carcinoma and potentially malignant lesions (red or white patches) should be biopsied promptly [15].

**Referral**: this patient is best managed in a specialist centre. Initially, with limited trismus, dental treatment remains feasible in general practice. As opening restricts, restorative and even preventive treatment becomes compromised — institute thorough preventive treatment as early as possible [16].

**Later-stage dental management**: extraction of teeth with even small carious lesions or moderate periodontitis may eventually become necessary, left until the last possible moment. Retain a stable occlusion to prevent permanent overclosure [16].
problems.prognosis:
Fibrosis is irreversible and may be progressive [5]. Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma occurs in 5–8% of cases [11]. In the late stages, patients may be unable to open the mouth at all, and incisor extractions may be required to allow feeding [17].

The prognosis for oral carcinoma developing in a patient with submucous fibrosis is very poor, mostly because the restricted opening makes examination, detection, and treatment extremely difficult, leading to late diagnosis [17].

citations.quote: This is a condition found particularly in those of South Asian origin. It is characterized by chronic and progressive scarring of oral connective tissue due to hyperplasia of fibroblasts induced by chewing betel nuts (without tobacco). The addition of tobacco to areca nut and slake lime appears to ↑ the risk of developing SCC. The mucosa is pale, with constraining fibrous bands, and fibrosis of the submucosa occurs, making the lips and cheeks immobile and resulting in trismus. The histology may reveal epithelial atrophy and cellular atypia. Pathogenesis is unclear; ↑ levels of copper due to areca nut chewing leading to cross-linking of collagen by upregulation of lysyl oxidase and thus ↑ fibrosis and DNA damage.
The fibrosis involving deep muscle is consistent with the diagnosis of oral submucous fibrosis, and the overlying epithelium shows mild dysplasia.

A habit practised by many people in the Indian subcontinent, much of south-east Asia and some parts of Africa. The basic quid comprises pieces or paste of areca nut and slaked lime, wrapped and tied into a packet in a vine leaf. A variety of other components is usually added; the combination varies between regions, but tobacco is almost always included, together with flavouring agents such as cinnamon, cloves and ginger. The areca nut contains alkaloids, which have a psychoactive effect and make the habit addictive.

The earliest features are relatively subtle and nonspecific. There is typically burning of the mucosa and roughness, sometimes described as 'tiny vesicles'. All or part of the lining mucosa may be affected, and these symptoms associated with betel quid chewing should be regarded with the highest suspicion.
The irreversible causes of trismus, such as oral submucous fibrosis or ankylosis after trauma, may be progressive in their early stages and do not respond to currently available treatment strategies.

The presentation and features are characteristic of oral submucous fibrosis. Gradual limitation of mouth opening and restriction of tongue movements are seen in a betel quid user who shows typical mucosal blanching and fibrosis presenting as bands in the buccal mucosa.

The buccal and soft palate mucosae are paler than normal, although some mucosal pigmentation consistent with the patient's skin colour makes this less obvious. When the mouth is opened fully, thin white hard bands run vertically just below the buccal mucosa. These are just visible in the figure and are much more readily felt as hard ridges. Some of the less pale areas are red and atrophic.

The maximum voluntary mouth opening. The normal interincisal opening in an adult is approximately 35 mm. Measurement will provide a baseline reading against which to judge treatment efficacy or trismus progression. It will also indicate the feasibility of dental and other intraoral treatment.

There is no facial asymmetry or evidence of scars or inflammation around the joint. No tenderness can be elicited from the muscles of mastication. There are no clicks, crepitus or tenderness associated with the TMJ and no mandibular deviation on opening the mouth.

All the tissue between the epithelium and the underlying muscle is replaced by relatively acellular dense fibrous tissue. The superficial muscle is atrophic and is being replaced by fibrous tissue. Occasional residual muscle fibres lie in the fibrosis. This deeper tissue is uninflamed.

Approximately one-third of patients with submucous fibrosis have oral white patches, and dysplasia is present in the mucosa of up to 16%. Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma occurs in 5–8% of cases.

This patient has limited mouth opening, most likely as a consequence of fibrosis in the masticatory muscles. Similar changes may also result from scarring after surgery. If trismus were of recent onset and progressive, there would be a suspicion that it may be caused by tumour infiltrating the muscles and thus indicate recurrence; otherwise, radiation is the likely cause.

No treatment regimen yields satisfactory results, and the aim is maintenance of oral health and prevention of complications. If patients are committed to mouth opening exercises, they may be spared the worst effects of extreme trismus. However, if disease is advanced at diagnosis, progressive limitation is likely. The best results are seen in those who have relatively localized disease at diagnosis, perhaps limited to the site of quid placement.

Dental practitioners have an important role in the prevention of betel quid chewing just as in the prevention of smoking. The majority of those who regularly chew betel quid are from low socioeconomic groups and, at least in the UK, are often poorly informed about the health risks. Health education for chewers is most important and may need to be extended to other family members.
All abnormal mucosa must be regarded with the utmost suspicion and a biopsy performed.

In the small number of patients who develop oral submucous fibrosis, dental treatment involves difficult choices and would be best carried out in a specialist centre. Initially, with limited trismus, treatment is not a problem and could be readily performed in a general dental practice. However, some restorative treatment will be rendered impossible as restriction of mouth opening progresses, and a thorough and effective regimen of preventive treatment must be instituted as soon as possible. Extraction of teeth with even small carious lesions or moderate periodontitis may become necessary, although it should be left until the last possible moment.

The second significant feature is restricted mouth opening. This is often progressive and responds poorly to treatment. In the late stages of disease, the patient may be unable to open the mouth at all, and incisor extractions may be required to allow feeding. Limited opening is a major handicap in the diagnosis and treatment of malignancy and premalignant lesions. It makes examination, detection and treatment extremely difficult, and the prognosis for oral carcinoma in a patient with submucous fibrosis is very poor, mostly as a result of late diagnosis.

problems.description: Sudden or rapid-onset reduced mouth opening following recent dental surgery, infection around a third molar, or trauma — with pain in the jaw and difficulty eating.
problems.etiology:
Trismus is reduced mouth opening less than 35 mm caused by spasm or restriction of the muscles of mastication [1]. The common treatable causes are:

- **Post-surgical muscle spasm**: pain and muscle spasm following third-molar surgery or other procedures. Trismus here is due to pain and muscle spasm, and reduces with adequate analgesia [2].
- **Odontogenic infection spreading to masticatory muscles**: when infection (especially from a lower third molar) spreads into the pterygo-mandibular space, submasseteric space, or surrounding tissue spaces, the muscles of mastication become involved. Trismus is an important sign — it indicates that infection or inflammation has spread to involve the muscles [3].
- **Intramuscular injection of LA**: injection of local anaesthetic into the medial pterygoid muscle results in trismus that resolves spontaneously [4].
- **Drug reactions**: metoclopramide and phenothiazines can cause acute masseteric spasm (dystonic reactions), particularly in young women and children [5].

Other causes (less common, and requiring referral): radiotherapy-induced fibrosis, malignant infiltration of masticatory muscles, and true ankylosis [6, 7].
problems.presentation:
The clinical picture depends on the cause:

**Post-surgical:**

- Pain, swelling, and trismus are common sequelae of third-molar surgery [2]. Pain is often severe and responds best to NSAIDs.
- Opening usually limited but not absent; resolves as swelling and pain settle.

**Infective:**

- Restricted opening with facial swelling, tenderness, and pyrexia [3]. The patient may feel systemically unwell.
- Swelling around the lower border of the mandible or in the submandibular space is characteristic of third-molar-related space infection [8].
- Only 22 mm of opening in severe cases [9].
- Pus may be visible from under the operculum of a partially erupted third molar [10].

**Drug-induced:**

- Bizarre acute trismus with sudden onset in a young patient on metoclopramide or a phenothiazine [5]. No infection or swelling.
problems.results:
- **Mouth opening measurement**: document interincisal distance. Normal is approximately 35 mm; trismus is defined as less than 35 mm [1]. This provides a baseline.
- **Temperature**: pyrexia (>37.8°C) indicates systemic spread of infection and changes management — hospital admission is required [11].
- **Distinguish intra- vs extra-articular**: in extra-articular (muscle-based) trismus, lateral and protrusive movements are usually preserved. In intra-articular disease, all movements are restricted [12].
- **Radiograph**: DPT to identify third-molar angulation, bone loss, and the cause of infective trismus. For complex space infections, CT defines the extent.
- **Blood tests** if infection is suspected: white cell count, CRP. Lymphadenitis in the submandibular triangle or deep cervical chain also signals spread [9].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The key differential is between reversible muscle-based trismus and the irreversible forms:

- **Infective trismus is reversible** and resolves with treatment of the cause — drainage and antibiotics. Pericoronitis-related trismus resolves 3–6 days after effective treatment [13].
- **Post-surgical trismus** is also reversible. It should be monitored and reduce as healing progresses [14].
- **Oral submucous fibrosis-related trismus** is progressive and irreversible — the history of betel quid use and gradual onset over months to years distinguishes it [1].
- **Malignancy**: if trismus is of recent onset and progressive in a patient who has had prior radiotherapy or head and neck cancer, tumour infiltrating the masticatory muscles must be excluded [7].

The rule of thumb: infection-related trismus arrives fast (hours to a day or two), is painful, and comes with swelling and systemic features. Forcing the jaws open under anaesthetic is contraindicated — it risks spreading the infection [15].
problems.treatment:
**Post-surgical trismus**:

- NSAIDs are the first choice — pain responds best to these [2]. Peri-operative LA leaves patients pain-free for the duration.
- Swelling (and with it, trismus) reduced by high-dose peri-operative steroids [2].
- Monitor; it should reduce progressively as healing occurs [14].

**Infective trismus**:

- Drain the pus, remove the cause, give antibiotics where indicated [3].
- Submandibular space infection requires extraoral drainage (incision 2 cm below the lower border of the mandible) [16].
- Do not force the jaws open under anaesthesia — this spreads infection [15].
- If trismus prevents adequate LA access, general anaesthesia may be needed; fibreoptic-guided intubation may be required if the airway is compromised [17].
problems.prognosis:
Infective and post-surgical trismus is usually reversible [1]. Almost complete resolution of infective trismus should follow within 3–6 days of effective drainage and antibiotics [13]. Trismus from LA injection into muscle resolves spontaneously [4].

If trismus is associated with a malignancy or radiotherapy, the prognosis depends on the underlying disease [7].

citations.quote: Trismus is best defined as the clinical sign of limited mouth opening less than 35 mm, which can result from a wide variety of causes. Historically, the definition of trismus was 'spasm of the muscles of mastication', but the broader description of limited opening is more relevant clinically. Trismus is usually reversible and most often results from treatable causes such as trauma or infection. It can be associated with other clinical symptoms such as pain in the jaw and difficulty performing activities that involve opening the mouth, such as toothbrushing or eating. The irreversible causes of trismus, such as oral submucous fibrosis or ankylosis after trauma, may be progressive in their early stages and do not respond to currently available treatment strategies.

Pain can be quite severe and responds best to NSAIDs. Peri-operative LA works well and leaves patients pain-free but numb for the duration. Trismus is due to pain and muscle spasm and can be ↓ by adequate analgesia. Swelling can also be ↓ by high-dose peri-operative steroids.
Trismus is an important sign, indicating that the infection or inflammation has spread to involve the muscles of mastication.
Injection into a muscle (will result in trismus which resolves spontaneously).
Phenothiazines and metoclopramide are notorious for causing dystonic reactions in young women and children. Bizarre attacks of trismus due to masseteric spasm have been ascribed to metoclopramide.

Trismus (interincisal opening ~<40mm, is often due to limitation of movement due to spasm of muscles of mastication), this may be confused with ankylosis but does not affect the joint. It is much more common and complicates many oral surgical procedures; may follow trauma or infection, may be a manifestation of occult malignancy, or a response to treatment, e.g. radiotherapy.

This patient has limited mouth opening, most likely as a consequence of fibrosis in the masticatory muscles. Similar changes may also result from scarring after surgery. If trismus were of recent onset and progressive, there would be a suspicion that it may be caused by tumour infiltrating the muscles and thus indicate recurrence; otherwise, radiation is the likely cause.

This swelling appears to be in the submandibular space. The main infected tissue is not visible and lies around the submandibular gland deep to the body of the mandible. The swelling just spreads round the lower border of the mandible onto the face. Moderate trismus is typical. It is relatively common for this tissue space to be involved in pericoronitis.

The patient has moderate extraoral swelling of the facial soft tissues overlying the extraction socket and some early discolouration of the skin as a result of ecchymosis. There is trismus, and she is able to open her mouth to only 22 mm interincisal clearance. There are no palpable lymph nodes in the deep cervical chain or submandibular triangle.
Trismus hampers examination. The lower right third molar can be seen to be partially erupted, the operculum is swollen and pus exudes from below it on gentle probing.
She has a temperature of 37.8°C (normal temperature 36.8°C) and is therefore pyrexic.

In intra-articular causes, the joint is abnormal and translation of the condyle is usually the movement initially affected. Translation occurs in the upper joint space, which is where opening, protrusion and lateral excursion take place. As a result, if the cause is intra-articular, then movement is restricted in all directions.

Patients may often feel much better within a few hours, and a noticeable reduction in swelling, trismus, pain and pyrexia should be observed within 24 hours. Almost complete resolution should follow in 3–6 days.
The trismus is almost certainly related to the surgical trauma of extraction. The trismus should be monitored and should reduce.
General anaesthesia should not be used in an attempt to overcome trismus. Forcing the jaws open will spread the infection.
The submandibular space must be drained through an extraoral incision, ideally 2 cm below the lower border of the mandible (to avoid damage to the mandibular branch of the facial nerve).
General anaesthesia will be required to drain the swelling. Fibreoptic-guided intubation may be necessary because of trismus and infection around the airway.

problems.description: Jaw clicking that clears after a few millimetres of opening, sometimes progressing to a locked jaw that won't open fully — preauricular pain, worse on chewing.
problems.etiology: What happens is that the articular disc — the meniscus — gets displaced anteriorly, sitting forward of the condylar head instead of on top of it [1]. On opening, the condyle has to translate forward past the displaced disc; at 2–3 mm of tooth separation the disc snaps back onto the condyle and you hear the click [1]. The reason a click can progress to a lock is mechanical: if the disc fails to reduce — if it doesn't snap back — the condyle is blocked from full forward translation, and the jaw is locked in a partially open position [1]. The same parafunctional habits (bruxism, clenching) may be upstream causes, though this does not fully explain the high incidence of internal derangement [2].
problems.presentation:
The classic sequence:

- **Early**: a click at 2–3 mm of opening and sometimes on closing, painless or with mild preauricular discomfort [1].
- **Progressive**: the click becomes louder or more frequent, and preauricular pain on chewing or wide opening develops.
- **Late**: a lock — the jaw jams at reduced opening (typically 25–35 mm), the click disappears because the disc is now permanently displaced, and attempts to open further hit a hard mechanical block [1].

Some patients report transient locking that resolves with a jaw wiggle; others present with acute, persistent lock.
problems.results:
- **Clicking**: present at 2–3 mm of tooth separation on opening and sometimes closing [1]. Diagnostic.
- **Limited opening**: in an acute lock, interincisal distance is typically reduced.
- **Palpation**: tenderness over the preauricular region [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The click at 2–3 mm of opening is the hallmark of reducing disc displacement — no other TMJ diagnosis produces this specific mechanical event [1]. When the disc stops reducing, the click disappears and is replaced by a fixed or intermittent lock: this transition from clicking to locking is diagnostic of progressive internal derangement. Myofascial pain-dysfunction syndrome (muscles-001) often co-exists but has no click and no mechanical block. TMJ osteoarthrosis produces crepitus (grating), not a defined click. Dislocation locks the mouth open, not closed. Ankylosis is severe, gradual, and has a childhood trauma or infection history.
problems.treatment:
Conservative first — the same measures that work for myofascial TMD work here [3]:

- Reassurance: most clicking joints do not progress and are not harmful.
- Splint therapy, analgesia, gentle heat, and exercises [3].
- If pain resolves but the patient is bothered by a persistent painful click or by recurrent locking, consider arthrocentesis or arthroscopy: irrigation of the upper joint space, lysis and lavage of adhesions, and injection of steroids and LA [4]. Published success rates exceed 90% [4].
- Open surgical options (meniscopexy, menisectomy, condylar shave, eminectomy) are reserved for refractory cases [4].
problems.prognosis: Most cases are self-limiting with conservative management [3]. Arthrocentesis and arthroscopy have surprisingly high success rates when conservative measures fail [4]. The takeaway: reassure first, operate last.

This is compatible with the observed high association with depression, back pain, tension headache, migraine, irritable bowel syndrome, and fibromyalgia. It does not, however, explain the cause in those patients who can identify no different levels of stress in their lives nor does it help explain the high incidence of internal derangement of the meniscus.

These three simple measures should relieve symptoms in ~80% of patients and identify those needing referral to a specialist (Fig. 11.7). Do not persist with ineffective Rx if symptoms have not improved within 3 months.

If pain can be abolished by other methods and the patient continues to be bothered by a painful click, particularly with recurrent locking, Rx aimed specifically at the meniscus is justified. The first line which may be useful diagnostically and improve pain due to capsulitis is arthrocentesis or arthroscopy. This includes irrigation of the upper joint space, through which lysis and lavage of adhesions and synovial inflammatory mediators, and injection of steroids and LA can be performed. These techniques have surprisingly high published success rates (>90%). The next line of surgical Rx includes open procedures such as meniscopexy, menisectomy, condylar shave, and eminectomy.

problems.description: Severely restricted or absent jaw opening — jaw feels fixed, won't open at all — usually in a patient with a history of childhood jaw fracture or a serious joint infection.
problems.etiology:
True ankylosis is bony or fibrous union within the joint itself, not external muscle spasm [1]. The usual backstory: an intracapsular fracture during childhood — when the condyle is still growing — heals with abnormal bony bridging across the joint space [1]. Infections (septic arthritis, osteomyelitis spreading to the joint) are the other main route [1].

Fibrous ankylosis is the earlier, softer stage — there is fibrous tissue bridging the joint but no solid bone. Bony ankylosis is the endpoint, where X-ray shows frank bony union [1]. What distinguishes true ankylosis from trismus at the bedside: trismus affects the muscles but leaves the joint intact; ankylosis is the joint itself that is obliterated [2].
problems.presentation:
Progressive restriction of mouth opening that may be traced back to a childhood trauma or serious infection. In bony ankylosis:

- Near-total or total absence of opening — the jaw simply doesn't move [1].
- No pain (the joint is fused — there is nothing to hurt).

In fibrous ankylosis:

- Some limited movement is possible and responds partially to passive stretching exercises.
problems.results:
- **Mouth opening**: extreme limitation, often under 10 mm interincisal clearance in bony ankylosis.
- **Imaging**: X-ray (OPG, CT) shows the degree of bony union across the condylar head and glenoid fossa — the condylar outline is lost in full bony ankylosis [1]. CT gives the clearest picture of bony architecture and guides surgical planning.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The key separation from trismus (muscles-003): trismus is extra-articular (muscles spasm, but translation of the condyle is possible to some degree) and is reversible; true ankylosis is intra-articular (the joint space is obliterated) and is irreversible without surgery [1, 2]. The childhood trauma or infection history, total absence of opening with no pain, and X-ray evidence of bony union within the joint all point to ankylosis rather than trismus or myofascial restriction. Dislocation locks the mouth open; ankylosis locks it closed.
problems.treatment:
Fibrous union: jaw exercises may improve range of movement [1]. Bony union: surgery is required.

- **Interpositional arthroplasty**: the bony fusion mass is resected and a spacer material (e.g. temporalis fascia, cartilage, alloplastic material) is interposed to prevent re-ankylosis [1].
- **Condylectomy with reconstruction**: when condylar anatomy is fully obliterated, the condyle is removed and reconstructed [1].
- **Post-operative exercise is crucial**: without aggressive physiotherapy immediately after surgery, re-ankylosis is likely [1].
problems.prognosis: Fibrous ankylosis treated with exercises can improve. Bony ankylosis requires surgery and carries a real risk of re-ankylosis if post-operative physiotherapy is inadequate [1].

citations.quote: True ankylosis is restriction of movement caused by a pathological joint condition, usually due to trauma (intracapsular # in childhood) or infection. Extreme limitation of movement and X-rays will confirm degree of bony union. In fibrous union, exercises are of value. In bony union, interpositional arthroplasty or condylectomy with reconstruction is needed. Post-operative exercise is crucial.

Restriction of movement imposed by extra-articular abnormalities is very rare. Rx depends upon cause. Trismus (interincisal opening ~<40mm, is often due to limitation of movement due to spasm of muscles of mastication), this may be confused with ankylosis but does not affect the joint. It is much more common and complicates many oral surgical procedures; may follow trauma or infection, may be a manifestation of occult malignancy, or a response to treatment, e.g. radiotherapy.

problems.description: Mouth stuck wide open after a wide yawn, dental procedure, or other wide-opening event — patient cannot close the jaw, condyle palpable in front of the ear.
problems.etiology: Dislocation happens when the condyle translates too far forward and comes to rest anterior to the articular eminence — and then can't get back [1]. The reason it gets stuck: the elevator muscles go into spasm with the jaw in the open position, which pulls the condyle up against the anterior slope of the eminence and locks it there. Two populations are at risk. First, patients with normal joints who experience an exceptional wide-opening event (yawn, prolonged dental procedure, general anaesthesia). Second, patients with lax ligaments, where dislocation becomes recurrent [1].
problems.presentation:
The patient presents with:

- Mouth locked wide open — they cannot close it [1].
- Bilateral or unilateral presentation. Bilateral is more dramatic.
- The condyle is palpable as a hard lump anterior to the articular eminence, where it shouldn't be [1].
- Speech is difficult; drooling is common.
- Significant pain and muscle spasm.

Acute dislocation is unmistakeable. Chronic recurrent dislocation is a different presentation: the patient may have learned to self-reduce and comes in with a history of repeated episodes.
problems.results:
- **Clinical**: condyle palpable anterior to articular eminence, mouth locked open [1].
- **X-ray**: confirms position of condyle anterior to eminence and rules out associated fracture [1].
- **Reduction**: immediate manual reduction is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Successful reduction confirms dislocation rather than fracture-dislocation.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The only condition in this origin where the mouth locks open rather than closed. Ankylosis locks it closed; trismus limits opening; internal derangement blocks full opening — none of these leaves the mouth stuck wide. The palpable condyle anterior to the eminence is pathognomonic.
problems.treatment:
Immediate manual reduction [1]:

- Place thumbs over the molar teeth (or in the buccal sulcus if LA is used — this avoids being bitten on reduction) and exert firm downward and backward pressure [1].
- LA around the dislocated joint and/or intravenous sedation reduces muscle spasm and allows reduction with less force [1].
- Advise jaw support when yawning after reduction.

For recurrent dislocation:

- Patients can be taught to self-reduce [1].
- Jaw exercises are of limited benefit but may reduce frequency [1].
- Sclerosant injections tighten the capsule and reduce recurrence [1].
problems.prognosis: Acute dislocation reduces well with prompt management [1]. Recurrent dislocation is problematic — conservative measures have limited efficacy, and some patients require surgical intervention. Intermaxillary fixation (IMF) is best avoided where possible [1].

citations.quote: Occurs in normal joints due to exceptional circumstances, or in lax joints where dislocation is recurrent. May be unilateral or bilateral. Condyle can be palpated anterior to articular eminence, X-rays confirm position, mouth is gagged open. Rx: immediate reduction; the vast majority can be performed with LA around the dislocated joint &/or sedation. Place thumbs over molar teeth and exert downward and backward pressure (if LA is used, less force is needed and thumbs can be placed in buccal sulcus, avoiding the risk of being bitten). Advise jaw support when yawning, etc.; this is usually enough, and avoids IMF. In chronically recurring dislocations, patients can be taught to self-reduce. Exercises are of limited benefit but may avoid surgery. Sclerosant injections are unpl

problems.description: Slowly worsening facial asymmetry in a young person — chin deviating to one side, bite not matching — with no pain, and the jaw still opening normally.
problems.etiology: Condylar hyperplasia is a rare, self-limiting condition of excessive unilateral condylar growth that persists beyond the normal growth period [1].
problems.presentation: Progressive, unilateral facial asymmetry in a teenager or young adult [1]. Normal or near-normal mouth opening — there is no mechanical restriction.
problems.results: - **Bone scintigraphy (technetium scan)**: the key functional investigation — confirms whether growth is still active. Interpretation can be variable [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The bone scan determines whether hyperplasia is active or burnt out, and guides surgical timing [1]. Only when the scan is cold — growth stopped — is definitive orthognathic correction appropriate.
problems.treatment:
The treatment decision turns on whether growth is still active [1]:

- **Active hyperplasia (hot bone scan)**: high condylectomy — removes the abnormally growing condyle head. Condylar replacement (e.g. with costochondral cartilage) may be needed, though outcomes are unpredictable [1].
- **Burnt-out hyperplasia (cold scan, growth stopped)**: wait, then perform definitive orthognathic surgery to correct the resulting facial asymmetry and malocclusion [1].
- Orthognathic surgery before growth stops will simply relapse as the condyle continues to enlarge.
problems.prognosis: Condylar hyperplasia is eventually self-limiting — growth burns out [1]. The residual deformity depends on how long the condition was active before treatment.

citations.quote: Rare. Rx: high condylectomy if active (bone scan, but interpretation variable and condylar replacement, e.g. with costochondral cartilage, is unpredictable) or wait for it to 'burnout', then definitive orthognathic surgery.

problems.description: TMJ pain, stiffness, and grating on movement in a patient known to have rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or gout.
problems.etiology: Rheumatoid, psoriatic, and gouty arthritides all manifest in the TMJ, but only in fewer than 15% of patients with the systemic disease [1]. In rheumatoid arthritis, the process is immunologically mediated: pannus (inflammatory synovial tissue) forms and erodes the articular surfaces [2]. Psoriatic arthritis is seronegative and usually milder in the TMJ [3]. Gout deposits urate crystals in the joint, causing acute severe pain [4].
problems.presentation:
What you'll hear:

- Joint stiffness and pain in the TMJ, worst in the morning [1].
- Tenderness directly over the joint on palpation.
- Crepitus (grating) on movement, more prominent than in myofascial TMD [1].

The systemic context is the anchor: these patients already have a known rheumatological diagnosis, and TMJ symptoms appear as one more joint in a polyarticular disease [1].
problems.results:
- **Inflammatory markers**: elevated ESR and CRP reflect systemic disease activity. Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP are positive in RA. Serum uric acid is elevated in gout.
- **Limited opening**: present in advanced disease; all movements restricted because the joint itself is diseased [5].
problems.definingCharacteristics:
The known systemic arthritis diagnosis is what makes this entry coherent. Without that context, these signs would look like TMJ osteoarthrosis or internal derangement. The separators:

- **From osteoarthrosis**: inflammatory arthritis is bilateral and systemic; osteoarthrosis is more focal and self-limiting.
- **From myofascial TMD**: inflammatory arthritis produces true articular crepitus and X-ray erosions; myofascial TMD has a normal joint on imaging.
- **Acute gout**: sudden severe pain with a crystal-depositing history and elevated uric acid distinguishes it from the chronic erosive pattern of RA and psoriatic arthritis.
problems.treatment:
The primary target is the systemic disease — treat that well and the TMJ often improves [1].

- Follow the rheumatologist's lead on disease-modifying drugs (methotrexate, TNFα inhibitors for RA) [2].
- Symptomatic management of the TMJ: splints, physiotherapy, jaw exercises, NSAIDs, and intra-articular steroids [1].
- The goal is limitation of functional decline — pain relief and maintenance of opening are the realistic targets [1].
problems.prognosis: The main long-term problem is limitation of function [1]. Keeping systemic disease under control is the best lever available for limiting TMJ progression.

citations.quote: Rheumatoid, psoriatic, and gouty arthritides all manifest in the TMJ but in <15% of patients with the systemic disease. The signs and symptoms are joint stiffness, pain, tenderness, and crepitus. ∆: knowledge of systemic disease and local signs. Rx: treat systemic condition. Symptomatic Rx of joint with appliances, physiotherapy, exercises, NSAIDs and intra-articular steroids. Main long-term problem is limitation of function.

(…… Rheumatoid arthritis, p. 544). Main associations are Sjögren syndrome (15%) and rheumatoid of the TMJ (10% cases), which may cause pain, swelling, and limitation of movement. Rarely, pannus formation within the joint may occur. Rx: as for systemic rheumatoid arthritis, which may include methotrexate or TNFα.

Associated with the skin condition and affects the spine and pelvis. It is usually milder than rheumatoid arthritis and has no serological abnormalities. The TMJ can be affected, but symptoms are usually mild despite some isolated case reports to the contrary.

Urates are deposited in joints, causing sudden severe joint pain, often in the great toe. Affected joints are red, swollen, and very tender. Gout 2° to drugs, radiotherapy, or haematological disease is commoner than that caused by an inborn error of metabolism.

In intra-articular causes, the joint is abnormal and translation of the condyle is usually the movement initially affected. Translation occurs in the upper joint space, which is where opening, protrusion and lateral excursion take place. As a result, if the cause is intra-articular, then movement is restricted in all directions.

problems.description: Grating jaw noise with limited and painful opening in a middle-aged or older patient — no systemic joint disease — that gradually improves over a couple of years.
problems.etiology: Osteoarthrosis of the TMJ is a distinct entity from osteoarthritis elsewhere — it has a different and more favourable natural history [1]. The source describes it simply as a degenerative condition of articular cartilage [1]. What makes this interesting is that unlike osteoarthrosis elsewhere, the TMJ version follows a different and more favourable clinical course — most patients have symptoms for around a year that gradually settle over the next two, and X-rays show the condyle remodelling to a flat smooth surface before a long period of remission [1].
problems.presentation:
- Crepitus — a grating or crunching sound on jaw movement — is the cardinal symptom [1]. This is different from the discrete click of disc displacement.
- Limited and painful opening, often with tenderness directly over the condyle on palpation [1].
- Pain on chewing, worsened by hard foods.
- No morning stiffness, no systemic features.
problems.results:
- **X-ray (OPG, cone-beam CT)**: condylar erosions, loss of condylar convexity, flattening of the condylar surface, subchondral sclerosis [1]. As the disease remits, X-rays show progressive remodelling toward a flat, smooth condylar surface [1].
- **Normal blood tests**: ESR, CRP, rheumatoid factor all normal — this separates it from inflammatory arthritis.
- **Crepitus on examination**: palpation of the joint during opening reveals the grating quality of the movement.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Crepitus rather than clicking is the acoustic signature — this separates osteoarthrosis from internal derangement (which clicks at 2–3 mm). The self-limiting natural history separates it from rheumatoid arthritis (progressive destructive joint disease). Normal inflammatory markers separate it from all the inflammatory arthritides. The condylar erosions on X-ray confirm articular surface loss — something myofascial TMD never produces. So actually, the X-ray is the key differentiator: normal in myofascial pain, erosive in osteoarthrosis.
problems.treatment:
Aimed at pain relief while the joint remodelds naturally [1]:

- Standard TMD measures: reassurance, analgesia (NSAIDs), splint therapy, gentle exercises.
- Intra-articular steroid injections for patients unresponsive to conservative measures — these probably accelerate the natural remodelling process [1].
- A small minority with severe, persistent symptoms may ultimately require joint replacement, but this is a last resort reserved for specialists [1].
problems.prognosis: Most patients have symptoms for roughly one year, which then gradually reduce over the next two years, with eventual remission and condylar remodelling to a flat smooth surface [1]. The natural history is favourable. A small group will remain with pain three to four years out and may need further intervention [1].

citations.quote: A distinct entity of the TMJ, with a different clinical course from that seen in other joints. Appears to be a degenerative condition of articular cartilage. ∆: crepitus, limitation, and pain on movement, tenderness over condyle, often with X-ray evidence of condylar erosions. Most have symptoms for ~1yr which gradually ↓ over the next 2yrs. X-rays show condylar remodelling to a flat smooth surface. Patients then enter a long period of remission. Rx is therefore aimed at pain relief, using standard TMD measures (…… Temporomandibular pain—dysfunction/facial arthromyalgia, p. 484). Those remaining unresponsive may benefit from intra-articular steroids (…… Intra-articular steroids, p. 602), which probably accelerate natural remodelling. A small group will remain with pain 3–4

problems.description: Restricted mouth opening with a stiff, waxy face in a woman with Raynaud's phenomenon and difficulty swallowing.
problems.etiology: Systemic sclerosis is a chronic connective tissue disease driven by diffuse fibrosis of skin and internal organs [1]. The reason the face and jaw are affected: perioral and buccal fibrosis thickens and tightens the skin and submucosal tissues, directly limiting mouth opening and altering the facial appearance [1]. Autoantibodies are present, and circulating markers like E-selectin and thrombomodulin are used to monitor disease activity [1]. It predominantly affects women aged 30–50 [1].
problems.presentation:
What you'll see:

- A waxy, mask-like facial appearance — classically described as a 'Mona Lisa face' [1]. Facial expression is reduced because the skin has lost elasticity.
- Restricted mouth opening due to perioral fibrosis; patients may struggle to open wide enough for dental treatment.
- Raynaud's phenomenon: painful, reversible digital ischaemia on cold exposure — often one of the earliest symptoms [1].
- Dysphagia from oesophageal involvement [1].
- Eating difficulties as jaw and perioral mobility deteriorates [1].
problems.results:
- **Reduced interincisal opening**: measure and document — provides a baseline and shows progression.
- **Perioral skin**: tight, indurated, with loss of normal skin folds and puckering around the mouth.
- **Autoantibodies**: anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I) and anti-centromere antibodies are the characteristic serological markers; autoantibodies confirmed on blood testing [1].
- **No articular clicking or crepitus**: the joint is structurally normal — restriction is perioral and soft tissue, not intra-articular.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The hallmark combination: restricted opening + waxy mask-like facies + Raynaud's phenomenon + dysphagia — all in a woman of working age. No other condition in this origin produces this quartet. Unlike myofascial TMD, the restriction here is from skin and soft tissue fibrosis, not muscle spasm; there is no tenderness of the muscles of mastication. Unlike inflammatory arthritis, the joint space itself is normal. The autoantibody screen confirms systemic sclerosis.
problems.treatment:
Systemic sclerosis has no cure; management is systemic and supportive [1].

- Cyclophosphamide and steroids may help in early disease [1]; penicillamine has been used but carries significant unwanted effects [1].
- Mouth opening exercises and physiotherapy to maintain as much jaw mobility as possible for as long as possible.
- Dental treatment: prioritise preventive treatment early — as opening restricts, access for restorative and surgical procedures becomes impossible. Refer to specialist centres for complex care.
problems.prognosis: Five-year survival is approximately 70% [1]. The oral and jaw restriction is progressive and not reversible. The practical implication for dentistry: treat early, treat preventively, and plan for the eventual inability to carry out routine dentistry as fibrosis advances.

citations.quote: A chronic disease characterized by diffuse sclerosis of connective tissues. F >  (30–50yrs). It has an insidious onset and is often associated with Raynaud's phenomenon (painful, reversible digital ischaemia on exposure to cold). Classically, the face has a waxy mask-like appearance ('Mona Lisa face'). Eating becomes difficult due to immobility of underlying tissues, and dysphagia occurs due to oesophageal involvement. Autoantibodies are present. Circulating levels of E-selectin and thrombomodulin are useful markers in monitoring disease activity. Rx: a combination of cyclophosphamide and steroids may help in early disease; penicillamine has always been used but has numerous unwanted effects. The 5yr survival is 70%.

problems.description: TMJ pain, swelling, and restricted opening in a patient already diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis — particularly when pannus formation is suspected.
problems.etiology: Rheumatoid arthritis is an immunologically mediated polyarthritis where joint pain and damage are the dominant features [1]. The TMJ is involved in around 10% of RA cases — but actual TMJ symptoms are rare, even though up to 15% of patients show radiographic changes in the condyle [2]. The mechanism is the same as in peripheral joints: synovial inflammation produces pannus — a mass of proliferating synovial tissue — which erodes the articular cartilage and subchondral bone [2].
problems.presentation:
- TMJ pain, swelling, and morning stiffness — the same pattern as affected peripheral joints [1].
- Limited opening, with all movements restricted because the joint itself is diseased [3].
- Systemic features: morning stiffness in hands and feet, symmetrical joint involvement, systemic upset, anaemia [1].
- Dry eyes and mouth if secondary Sjögren syndrome is present [2].
- Ulnar deviation of the fingers is pathognomonic for RA [1].
problems.results:
- **X-ray/CT**: condylar erosions, loss of joint space, subchondral sclerosis — indistinguishable radiographically from RA peripheral joint changes.
- **Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP**: positive in seropositive RA [1].
- **ESR and CRP**: elevated, reflecting systemic inflammatory activity.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The confirmed RA diagnosis is what distinguishes this from idiopathic TMJ osteoarthrosis or myofascial pain. The important clinical point: TMJ symptoms in RA patients should not be dismissed as unrelated — they are part of the systemic disease and should be co-managed with the rheumatologist. Pannus formation, though rare, warrants imaging [2].
problems.treatment:
Treat the systemic RA — this is the primary lever [2].

- NSAIDs, steroids, DMARDs (methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine), and biologics (TNFα inhibitors such as infliximab) per the rheumatologist's plan [1, 2].
- Symptomatic TMJ management: splints, physiotherapy, jaw exercises, NSAIDs, intra-articular steroids [2].
- Dental treatment: be aware of restricted opening when planning restorative work.
problems.prognosis: With good systemic disease control, TMJ involvement often stabilises. Pannus-driven condylar destruction is the worst-case scenario and may result in severe malocclusion requiring surgical correction. The prognosis for TMJ function tracks closely with systemic disease activity.

citations.quote: Immunologically mediated disease where joint pain and damage are the most prominent symptoms. Morning pain and stiffness in the hands and feet, usually symmetrical, is characteristic. There may be systemic upset and anaemia. Ulnar deviation of the fingers is pathognomonic. Rx includes NSAIDs, steroids, and physiotherapy. Second-line or disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) may favourably influence outcome at expense of unwanted effects, e.g. penicillamine, antimalarials, immunosuppressants (including TNFα chimeric monoclonal antibody—infliximab). Dry eyes and mouth may be associated with rheumatoid arthritis (…… Sjögren syndrome (secondary Sjögren syndrome), p. 460). TMJ symptoms are rare in rheumatoid arthritis, although up to 15% of patients have radiographic ch

(…… Rheumatoid arthritis, p. 544). Main associations are Sjögren syndrome (15%) and rheumatoid of the TMJ (10% cases), which may cause pain, swelling, and limitation of movement. Rarely, pannus formation within the joint may occur. Rx: as for systemic rheumatoid arthritis, which may include methotrexate or TNFα.

In intra-articular causes, the joint is abnormal and translation of the condyle is usually the movement initially affected. Translation occurs in the upper joint space, which is where opening, protrusion and lateral excursion take place. As a result, if the cause is intra-articular, then movement is restricted in all directions.

problems.description: Severely restricted mouth opening in a child — jaw progressively stiffer over months to years, with or without facial growth asymmetry.
problems.conditionName: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (TMJ ankylosis in children)
problems.etiology: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) — also called juvenile rheumatoid arthritis or Still's disease — is the childhood counterpart of RA, and it can be much more severe in its joint consequences [1]. In severe cases it can cause TMJ ankylosis [1].
problems.presentation:
- Restricted mouth opening developing in childhood — insidious onset, progressive.
- In severe cases, near-total loss of opening (ankylosis) [1].
- Morning stiffness and joint tenderness may or may not be prominent.
problems.results:
- **Reduced interincisal opening**: document in millimetres as a baseline.
- **Imaging**: X-rays will confirm degree of bony union if ankylosis develops [2].
problems.definingCharacteristics: JIA can cause TMJ ankylosis in children [1], which follows the same principles as post-traumatic ankylosis [2]. JIA can be much more severe than adult RA.
problems.treatment:
Systemic treatment of JIA under the paediatric rheumatologist — early aggressive treatment limits joint damage [1].

- Regular dental monitoring: measure mouth opening at each visit for any child with known JIA.
- Jaw physiotherapy and exercises to maintain opening.
- For established TMJ ankylosis in children: surgical management follows the same principles as post-traumatic ankylosis — interpositional arthroplasty or condylectomy with reconstruction [2].
- Post-operative physiotherapy is crucial to reduce risk of re-ankylosis [2].
problems.prognosis: JIA can be much more severe than adult RA and its joint consequences more lasting [1]. Established ankylosis requires surgery and carries risk of re-ankylosis.

citations.quote: Rarer form of the disease affecting children. It can be much more severe than the adult condition and can cause TMJ ankylosis.

True ankylosis is restriction of movement caused by a pathological joint condition, usually due to trauma (intracapsular # in childhood) or infection. Extreme limitation of movement and X-rays will confirm degree of bony union. In fibrous union, exercises are of value. In bony union, interpositional arthroplasty or condylectomy with reconstruction is needed. Post-operative exercise is crucial.

problems.description: Limited jaw opening and spine stiffness in a young man, worsening slowly — back worse in the mornings, improves with movement.
problems.etiology: Ankylosing spondylitis is a seronegative inflammatory arthritis that primarily affects the spine and sacroiliac joints in young men, strongly associated with HLA-B27 [1]. The inflammation targets the insertion points of ligaments and tendons (enthesitis) rather than synovium alone. The same process can affect the TMJ.
problems.presentation:
- Progressive spinal stiffness — worst in the mornings, easing with movement [1]. This is the opposite of mechanical back pain.
- Limited jaw opening as TMJ involvement develops — the degree of restriction varies.
- Kyphotic deformity of the spine in advanced cases [1].
- Associated increased risk of cervical fracture in late disease due to ankylotic bone being brittle [1].
problems.results:
- **HLA-B27**: positive in most cases.
- **Normal or mildly elevated inflammatory markers**: ESR and CRP may be elevated during active disease but can be normal.
- **Rheumatoid factor**: negative (seronegative arthritis) [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: The spinal picture is the primary differentiator — limited jaw opening in a young man with morning back stiffness, HLA-B27 positivity, and sacroiliitis is a different presentation from any other entry in this origin. The TMJ involvement is a component of a systemic seronegative arthritis, not an isolated joint problem. Unlike RA, it is seronegative, affects the axial skeleton predominantly, and occurs in young men.
problems.treatment:
Treat the systemic disease:

- Physiotherapy and spinal exercises are critical to maintain posture and mobility [1].
- TMJ management: standard symptomatic measures — splints, jaw exercises, analgesics.
- Beware of cervical spine fragility when positioning patients in the dental chair in advanced disease.
problems.prognosis: Ankylosing spondylitis follows a variable course — many patients maintain good function with treatment and exercise. Progressive spinal fusion in untreated disease produces the classic kyphotic deformity and brittle spine [1]. TMJ restriction tracks with systemic disease activity and may plateau. Cervical fracture risk in advanced disease is a real concern — patients need to be aware.

citations.quote: Affects the spine, usually in young men. Inflammation involves the insertion of ligaments and tendons. It is associated with HLA-B27. Later, kyphotic deformity and ↑ risk of cervical fractures.

problems.description: Jaw claudication — aching that builds on chewing and forces the patient to stop — in an older person with a sore, tender temple and a raised ESR.
problems.etiology:
Polymyalgia rheumatica is a generalised vasculitis affecting proximal axial muscles and is closely related to cranial arteritis — accounting for 25% of temporal arteritis cases [1, 2]. The reason jaw claudication occurs: the underlying pathology is inflammatory arteritis affecting the vascular supply to the jaw muscles [2]. Temporal arteritis itself causes throbbing headache localised to the temporal and frontal regions, with a tender, pulseless temporal artery on examination [2].

The condition affects older people — average age of onset 70 years — and is a genuine dental emergency because the major risk is retinal artery involvement, which can cause sudden permanent blindness [2].
problems.presentation:
What you'll hear:

- Jaw claudication: aching pain on chewing that builds rapidly and forces the patient to stop, then eases at rest [2]. This is pathognomonic for masseteric ischaemia.
- Temporal and frontal headache — severe, described as a severe ache [2].
- The temporal artery on the affected side may be visibly thickened, nodular, and tender to palpation.
- General malaise, shoulder girdle pain, and morning stiffness (polymyalgia component) [1].
- Scalp tenderness.
problems.results:
- **ESR**: very high — the key screening test and disease activity monitor [2].
- **CRP**: also elevated.
- **Temporal artery**: pulseless, tender, and thickened on palpation [2].
- **Biopsy**: temporal artery biopsy confirms the diagnosis — shows fragmented elastic tissue with giant cell arteritis [2].
- **Vision**: any change in visual acuity is a red flag — ophthalmic involvement needs emergency ophthalmology referral.
problems.definingCharacteristics: Jaw claudication is the discriminating feature for this entry: it is not pain at rest, not pain from a dental cause, but muscle ischaemia pain that builds on exercise (chewing) and stops with rest. No other condition in this origin produces claudication-type jaw pain. Combine it with the age group (70s), the tender thickened temporal artery, and the very high ESR, and the diagnosis is clear. Delay is dangerous: optic nerve ischaemia causing blindness can follow within days if steroids are not started [2].
problems.treatment:
This is a medical emergency — start steroids immediately on clinical suspicion, before the biopsy result [2].

- High-dose prednisolone 60 mg daily orally [2]. Don't wait for biopsy: the biopsy remains positive for days to weeks after starting steroids.
- Monitor using ESR as the primary disease activity marker [2].
- Refer urgently to ophthalmology if any visual symptoms are present [2].
- Confirm diagnosis with temporal artery biopsy.
problems.prognosis: With prompt steroid treatment, the condition responds well and vision is usually preserved [2]. Delay risks irreversible blindness.

citations.quote: More generalized vasculitis affecting proximal axial muscles. Accounts for 25% of cases of cranial arteritis. Responds to steroids; gradual improvement with time.

This is a condition affecting older age groups (average age of onset 70yrs) and related to polymyalgia rheumatica. The pain is localized to the temporal and frontal regions and usually described as a severe ache, although it can be paroxysmal. The affected area is tender to touch. Jaw claudication is seen in 20%. Major risk is involvement of retinal arteries, with sudden deterioration and loss of vision; underlying pathology is inflammatory arteritis. Biopsy shows the arterial elastic tissue to be fragmented with giant cells. ∆: pulseless temporal arteries, classical distribution of pain, very high ESR. Rx: high-dose steroids (60mg prednisolone PO od) and monitor using ESR.

problems.description: Weakness and pain in the jaw and chewing muscles alongside proximal limb weakness — part of a broader inflammatory muscle disease with possible skin rash.
problems.etiology: Polymyositis is a generalised, immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of skeletal muscle [1]. The masticatory muscles are skeletal muscles, so they can be involved as part of the systemic disease. When a characteristic skin rash (heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules) accompanies the myositis, the condition is called dermatomyositis — and that variant carries an important association with occult malignancy [1].
problems.presentation:
- Proximal limb weakness — difficulty raising arms above the head, getting up from a chair — is the dominant symptom [1].
- Jaw muscle involvement produces weakness on chewing, difficulty managing hard foods, and sometimes pain in the masticatory muscles.
- Dysphagia if pharyngeal or oesophageal muscles are involved.
- In dermatomyositis: a characteristic skin rash accompanies the myositis [1].
- Systemic malaise, muscle tenderness.
problems.results: - Screen for occult malignancy in dermatomyositis [1].
problems.definingCharacteristics: Masticatory involvement in polymyositis is part of a generalized muscle disease — it is never an isolated finding. The separators from other entries in this origin: there is proximal limb weakness (nothing else here causes this); there are raised muscle enzymes; the pattern is systemic. The dermatomyositis variant with its skin findings and malignancy association makes it especially important to recognise. Unlike myofascial TMD, there is true muscle weakness rather than pain-driven restriction.
problems.treatment:
Treat the systemic disease — the masticatory component is a peripheral manifestation [1].

- Screen for occult malignancy in dermatomyositis — finding and treating an underlying cancer may resolve the myositis [1].
- Physiotherapy to maintain muscle function during treatment.
- Dental management: soft diet advice; assist with oral hygiene if jaw weakness limits brushing.
problems.prognosis: Polymyositis responds to immunosuppression in most cases, with gradual return of muscle strength. Dermatomyositis prognosis depends partly on whether an underlying malignancy is found and treated [1]. Long-term immunosuppression is usually required.

citations.quote: A generalized immune-mediated inflammatory disorder of muscle. If a characteristic rash is present the condition is known as dermatomyositis and has an association with occult malignancy.

problems.description: Repetitive involuntary movements of the face and jaw — grimacing, lip-smacking, tongue protrusion — in a patient on long-term antipsychotics or metoclopramide, or with Parkinson's disease.
problems.etiology:
Orofacial dyskinesia is a movement disorder producing repetitive, involuntary orofacial movements [1]. Two main routes:

- **Drug-induced (tardive dyskinesia)**: long-term exposure to dopamine-blocking drugs — phenothiazines (antipsychotics) and metoclopramide (antiemetic) — causes involuntary movements that can persist even after the drug is stopped [1]. Phenothiazines and metoclopramide are notorious for causing dystonic reactions, particularly in young women and children [1]. The metoclopramide variant can also cause acute masseteric spasm — bizarre attacks of trismus [1].
- **Parkinson's disease**: orofacial dyskinesia can manifest as part of the condition [1].
problems.presentation:
Repetitive, patterned, involuntary movements of the lower face:

- Lip-smacking, pursing, and puckering.
- Tongue protrusion (fly-catching movements), lateral tongue movements.
- Grimacing, jaw opening-closing, lateral jaw movement.
- These are constant or semi-constant, not triggered by touch or a specific stimulus (distinguishing them from trigeminal neuralgia).

In the acute dystonic variant (from metoclopramide): sudden severe jaw and neck muscle spasm — trismus or torticollis — within hours of the drug dose [1]. Very different presentation from the chronic tardive picture.
problems.results:
- **Drug history**: the pivotal investigation. Establish which drugs, at what dose, and for how long. Drug-induced tardive dyskinesia often appears after months to years of antipsychotic use.
- **Neurological examination**: assess for Parkinson's features (resting tremor, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity) to distinguish Parkinson's-related from drug-induced dyskinesia.
- **No structural dental cause**: all teeth and periodontal tissues are normal; the movements are not related to dental occlusion or TMJ disease.
problems.definingCharacteristics: The involuntary, repetitive, patterned nature of the movements is what sets this apart. No other entry in this origin produces spontaneous rhythmic orofacial movements. Trismus from metoclopramide is the acute variant — it has an abrupt onset tied to a drug dose — distinguishable from other causes of trismus by the drug history and absence of swelling, infection, or trauma. The combination of drug exposure + involuntary orofacial movements + no dental or TMJ pathology makes the diagnosis.
problems.treatment:
Drug-induced dyskinesia:

- Stop or reduce the offending drug if clinically possible [1].
- Tardive dyskinesia may persist after stopping — early recognition and dose reduction are the best preventive steps.
- Acute dystonic reactions (metoclopramide, phenothiazines): anticholinergic drugs reverse the acute spasm [1].
problems.prognosis: Acute dystonic reactions resolve promptly with anticholinergic treatment. Tardive dyskinesia is less predictable — may persist or be permanent even after stopping the offending drug, especially with prolonged antipsychotic exposure. Parkinson's dyskinesia fluctuates with disease progression and medication adjustments.

citations.quote: Tetanus is an obvious cause. Muscular dystrophy may present with ptosis and facial paralysis. Hemifacial spasm and other tics may be caused by a tumour at the cerebello-pontine angle. Orofacial dyskinesia can be a manifestation of Parkinson's disease or an unwanted effect of major tranquillizers. Phenothiazines and metoclopramide are notorious for causing dystonic reactions in young women and children. Bizarre attacks of trismus due to masseteric spasm have been ascribed to metoclopramide.
